third_paragraph.7: Compensation controls the returning echo near an individual reference frequency, which lies slightly above the resting frequency. An emission change and an echo-frequency error are different measurements, so a bat can make a large downward change in emitted frequency and still keep a small positive offset in its feedback.

8.add: Frequency and audibility are coupled in a sharply tuned hearing system, so a sound below the most sensitive band may have to be much louder to be equally audible, and the historical difference reflects a change in experimental conditions and interpretation.

10.add: The presence of an upward vocal correction establishes that feedback below the resting frequency can influence the control system, and the correction in that direction remained smaller.

11.add: The vocal apparatus must convert an auditory correction into a change in the call, and the authors proposed that laryngeal constraints contribute to the smaller upward range. The experiment measured vocal output during playback.

12.add: The time constant was measured from the vocal trajectory as progress toward the final correction, so it describes the behavior of the entire feedback loop, which includes the strength of the returning acoustic signal.

third_paragraph.13: Its endpoint is a change in CF emission, measured in frequency and over time, so the acoustic output provides a precise readout of the feedback correction in stationary bats. Imaging the vocal apparatus or recording motor neurons addresses the steps between the auditory discrepancy and the vocal adjustment.

15.add: The atlas provides a cellular framework for interpreting the peripheral specialization established by acoustic and electrophysiological experiments, with hair cells and supporting cells forming the sensory compartment and spiral ganglion neurons carrying cochlear information toward the brainstem.

third_paragraph.16: The plotted expression clusters are molecular groupings of nuclei. A cell's RNA profile identifies candidate functions, and a firing threshold, a preferred echo frequency or a contribution to vocal feedback would come from recordings of those cells.
third_paragraph.17: The atlas found two principal SGN categories, whose labels describe molecular populations. Linking an RNA identity to recordings of individual tuning curves is what would assign a specific cell population an echo-frequency computation, so an association between a molecular category and narrowly tuned CF processing is a proposal.
third_paragraph.18: KCNQ4 is a candidate cellular mechanism placed in a tissue context, and the molecular evidence complements peripheral recordings. Expressed genes, functional membrane currents and behavior are distinct levels of evidence, each measured by different experiments.

19.add: Differential expression describes a difference in measured gene abundance between comparison groups, and combining whole-tissue comparisons with single-nucleus localization separates a cochlear-wide molecular signal into candidate cellular sources.

20.add: Pathway networks are built from gene-expression categories, so their connections indicate relationships among annotated pathways, and calcium signaling occupies a central position in the horseshoe-bat network whereas the FM-bat comparison emphasizes a glutamatergic-synapse pathway.

third_paragraph.21: A shared gene framework improves comparability by giving the two species a common comparison space. The joint analysis separates shared cellular organization from species-associated expression differences, and a CF-associated expression pattern is a candidate adaptation to be tested with wider comparative sampling or direct manipulation.
third_paragraph.22: Molecular heterogeneity describes how RNA abundance varies across a cellular population. A relatively uniform RNA population could contain physiologically diverse neurons, and the molecular comparison motivates targeted electrophysiological tests of tuning in the corresponding neurons.

23.add: The pathway includes GABA A and GABA B receptor annotations, distinct receptor classes through which GABA can influence cellular signaling, so the atlas identifies candidate inhibitory roles that receptor-specific interventions and neuronal measurements can test.

24.add: Ligand–receptor inference predicts possible communication when one cell class expresses a signaling molecule and another expresses a corresponding receptor, and glial molecular specialization is a candidate contributor to the sensory environment of the cochlea.

25.add: The recorded CM onset, neural onset and neural offset signals had different best frequencies, and the displaced neural onset minimum was related to the time course of cochlear excitation, so a population onset measure reflects response timing as well as sensitivity.

28.add: Changing the duration and extent of the terminal sweep changed the outcome, so the CF and FM components are not independent sounds whose responses add, and a brief FM ending alters how the resonant system stops responding to CF stimulation.

29.add: The offset cluster could remain conspicuous at low levels or particular frequencies while the sustained response was much weaker, so the observation provides a cellular counterpart to the summed neural offset potential.

30.add: A reference defined from vocal emission need not coincide with a reference defined from the sensory response, which parallels the difference between resting and reference frequencies in behavioral compensation experiments.

31.add: Sharp duration tuning coexists with sharply tuned peripheral input, so the long cochlear ringing does not force every central response to be temporally broad.

32.add: Central processing can produce sharp temporal filtering despite a peripheral input specialized for narrowband frequency analysis, and neurons outside the specialized band displayed the more conventional relationship between frequency and duration tuning.

33.add: A single duration preference therefore depends on the carrier frequency at which it is measured, and the experiment supports an interaction between spectral input and central temporal processing.

third_paragraph.34: The authors considered temporally offset excitation and inhibition, including coincidence and anti-coincidence accounts, as a central filtering hypothesis for the frequency-dependent duration selectivity. Behavioral compensation and central duration tuning are separate measured phenomena, even though both depend on the specialized CF band.

35.add: Overlapping emitted CF signals and returning echoes can provide beat information, and the impulse timing supplies information beyond the average number of impulses produced by a tone, a potential temporal representation of frequency difference.

38.add: The stable frequency of the communication calls supports the proposal that their control differs from that of echolocation calls, with frequency regulation depending on vocal context instead of acoustic similarity alone.

39.add: This unequal allocation gives more space to intermediate preferred sound levels, and the author proposed a relation to the amplitudes of echoes commonly used in echolocation.

40.add: The echo frequency was calculated from the recorded call frequency and the reconstructed flight kinematics, so natural flight supplies a counterpart to the playback experiments, and the calculated echo frequency changed far less than the emitted frequency.

third_paragraph.42: The investigators paired the resting call series measured just before take-off with the echo estimate from that particular flight, because both frequencies can change across time. A precise control system can track a preferred state that itself changes, and a contemporaneous baseline distinguishes movement of the preferred band from error around that band.

43.add: The logger measured skin temperature, an indirect indicator of internal temperature, and activation changes more than temperature alone, so the resting-frequency baseline can vary even when the animal is stationary.

44.add: Internal tissues could warm earlier than the skin, and the later decline in both quantities supports their association while the temporal difference between their peaks remains.

third_paragraph.45: Afferent input carries sensory information into the nervous system, and efferent output changes the vocal apparatus, so the new call changes the acoustic feedback returning to the ear. The directly observed findings are the change in resting frequency, its relation to skin temperature and the coupling of resting and reference frequencies, and together the behavioral and peripheral studies constrain how a moving sensory target can remain compatible with precise echo regulation.

inserts.title: Calls contain harmonics at whole-number multiples
paragraphs: A harmonic belongs to a series of frequencies related by whole-number multiples of the lowest component. A bat call can contain several harmonics at once, and the amplitude of each harmonic differs, so one harmonic can dominate the energy of the call.

In recordings of Hipposideros armiger during flight, the second harmonic carried the greatest amplitude, with a constant-frequency component near 65–66 kHz, above the human audible range. Schoeppler and colleagues recorded stationary calling and flight toward a landing grid.

The sustained CF component remained present during the final approach, although the calls became shorter and the higher harmonics weakened. The CF and FM labels describe acoustic components of one call, so a narrowband carrier and a changing terminal sweep coexist within individual calls.
inserts.citation: Schoeppler et al. (2018); Suga et al. (1975)
notes: A call is a sound with several frequency components, and the labels CF and FM name parts of one call and do not name two calls.
Harmonics.
A harmonic belongs to a series of frequencies related by whole-number multiples.
The second harmonic was the strongest component in the Hipposideros armiger recordings.
Where the frequencies lie.
The second-harmonic CF component was near 65 to 66 kilohertz.
That frequency is above the human audible range.
Call structure during approach.
The sustained component remained present during the final approach.
The calls became shorter and the higher harmonics weakened.
CF and FM labels.
Constant frequency describes the sustained part of the call, and frequency modulation describes the brief change in frequency at its end.
The labels describe acoustic components of one call.
Why one harmonic dominates.
Each harmonic in a call has its own amplitude, so energy is not shared equally across the series.
In the flight recordings the second harmonic carried the most energy.
Reading the numbers.
A frequency near 65 to 66 kilohertz lies above what humans hear, so the call is inaudible to us even when it is intense.

inserts.title: Approach raises echo frequency
paragraphs: A Doppler shift is a change in frequency caused by relative motion between a sound source, a reflector and a receiver. When a bat approaches a stationary object, the returning echo has a higher frequency than the emitted call, because the bat's own motion changes the frequency that it receives.

The bat counters the shift by lowering the frequency of its later calls, so the returning CF frequency is the regulated quantity. The emitted CF frequency therefore changes during flight, and the bat can maintain a relatively stable echo frequency while producing calls whose frequencies differ substantially.

Schoeppler and colleagues reconstructed flight toward a grid, and call frequency fell during acceleration and recovered during deceleration. Schuller and colleagues changed only the frequency of the echo in stationary bats, which separates an effect of auditory feedback from the mechanical effects of flight.
inserts.citation: Schuller et al. (1974); Schoeppler et al. (2018)
notes: Compensation is an adjustment of the outgoing call based on the returning echo, and playback separates that feedback from the movement of the body.
Self-motion changes echo frequency.
A stationary reflector can return a frequency-shifted echo when the bat itself is moving.
Motion toward the reflector raises the returning frequency.
The adjustment.
The bat lowers the frequency it emits on later calls.
The echo frequency is therefore held relatively stable while the emitted frequency changes.
Evidence from flight.
Free-flight recordings connect the adjustment to natural movement.
Movement also changes distance and echo intensity, so flight alone does not isolate frequency feedback.
Evidence from playback.
A stationary animal changes its call frequency when only the frequency of its acoustic feedback is altered.
Physical acceleration is therefore not required to evoke the response.
Direction of the shift.
Approaching a stationary object raises the echo frequency above the emitted frequency.
The bat lowers later calls so that the returning frequency stays relatively stable.
Two experimental routes.
Flight reconstruction followed call frequency during acceleration and deceleration.
Playback to stationary bats changed only the echo, which separates auditory feedback from the mechanical effects of flight.

inserts.title: Resting and reference frequencies differ
paragraphs: The resting frequency is the mean CF frequency of consecutive calls from a stationary bat, and the reference frequency is the returning CF frequency maintained during compensation. They are two different baselines, one defined by the call that is emitted and the other by the echo that is received.

In Schuller and colleagues' experiments, the downward change in emission was slightly smaller than the upward shift imposed on the artificial echo, so the echo remained above the resting frequency. This compensation offset was approximately 50–300 Hz across the bats and stayed relatively constant across an individual's compensation range.

An emission change and an echo-frequency error are different measurements. A bat can make a large downward change in emitted frequency and still keep a small positive offset in its feedback, so the regulated echo band differs from the average call frequency measured at rest.
notes: Two baselines describe the same bat, one for what it emits and one for what it hears, and comparing them requires the same animal and the same time.
Resting frequency.
It is calculated from a series of calls made while the bat is stationary.
It is an individual baseline, not a single frequency for the entire species.
Reference frequency.
The authors called the stabilized returning frequency the reference frequency.
It lies slightly above the resting frequency.
Why the offset exists.
An artificial echo combines the emitted frequency with the shift added by the apparatus.
Lowering emission by slightly less than the added shift leaves the echo slightly above the resting baseline.
Size of the offset.
The offset was about 50 to 300 hertz depending on the animal and stayed similar across the imposed shifts within an animal.
Two baselines.
The resting frequency is defined from the call that is emitted, and the reference frequency is defined from the echo that is received.
Keeping them separate prevents an emission change from being read as an echo error.
Size of the offset.
The compensation offset was approximately 50 to 300 hertz across bats and stayed relatively constant within an individual.

inserts.title: Equal audibility tests the sign of the shift
paragraphs: A horseshoe bat's hearing is most sensitive in a narrow band near its preferred echo frequency, so the same physical sound level can be easily audible at one frequency and barely audible at another. Sensation level expresses how far a sound lies above the hearing threshold at its own frequency.

Early playback experiments found that downward shifts of artificial echoes did not systematically raise emitted frequency. Metzner and colleagues compared feedback above and below the resting frequency at comparable levels above hearing threshold, which required louder playback for the lower frequencies.

Under those conditions negative shifts did raise emitted frequency above the resting frequency, while positive shifts lowered it. The earlier asymmetry was therefore attributed to a difference in audibility between the two kinds of feedback, and lower-frequency echoes do take part in vocal control.
inserts.citation: Metzner et al. (2002); Schuller et al. (1974)
notes: A fair test of upward and downward shifts matches how audible the feedback is, because sensitivity depends strongly on frequency.
Audibility depends on frequency.
The narrow sensitive band of a horseshoe bat means that a sound below that band may need to be much louder to be equally audible.
Sound pressure level measures the sound itself and sensation level measures it relative to threshold.
The matched comparison.
Metzner and colleagues controlled playback level relative to hearing threshold.
Feedback was shifted above and below the animal's resting frequency.
The result.
Upward shifts caused emitted frequency to decrease.
Sufficiently audible downward shifts caused emitted frequency to increase above resting frequency.
Change of interpretation.
The historical difference is a change in experimental conditions and interpretation, and it does not reflect a new ability of the bat's nervous system between studies.
Sensation level.
Hearing is most sensitive in a narrow band near the preferred echo frequency, so equal sound pressure is not equally audible at different frequencies.
Sensation level states how far a sound lies above threshold at its own frequency.
Result of the comparison.
Louder playback was needed for the lower frequencies.
With that correction, negative shifts raised emitted frequency and positive shifts lowered it.

inserts.title: A time constant measures progress toward correction
paragraphs: A time constant describes how quickly a response approaches its final value. For a vocal correction it is measured from the trajectory of the emitted frequency, as progress toward the adjusted call frequency, and a shorter time constant means a faster correction.

Metzner and colleagues varied the attenuation of the echo mimic, the reduction in its signal level, while applying stepwise frequency perturbations. For recovery after a negative step, the time constant shortened from about 2.28 s at 30 dB attenuation to 0.89 s with no attenuation, and for positive steps from about 1.64 s to 0.75 s.

Stronger feedback therefore produced faster correction in both directions. A rule that used only the sign of the frequency error, without regard for audibility, would not predict response speeds that depend on feedback strength.
notes: The speed of correction measures how strongly the returning echo drives the vocal change.
Reading a time constant.
It is measured from the vocal trajectory as progress toward the final correction.
It is not a conduction delay in a single neuron.
Weaker feedback.
Attenuating an echo mimic by 30 decibels makes it weaker than the unattenuated playback.
Weaker feedback produced slower correction.
The measured values.
Recovery after a negative step shortened from about 2.28 s to 0.89 s as attenuation went from 30 dB to zero.
For positive steps the corresponding values shortened from about 1.64 s to 0.75 s.
What the result constrains.
The result constrains the behavior of the whole feedback loop, which includes the strength of the returning acoustic signal.
Reading a time constant.
A time constant describes progress toward the final value, so a shorter value means that the call frequency reached its correction faster.
It is measured from the trajectory of the emitted frequency.
Attenuation and speed.
Reducing the level of the echo mimic slowed recovery in both directions.
Positive steps recovered from about 1.64 to 0.75 seconds as attenuation was removed.

inserts.title: Cochlear microphonic and N1 sample different stages
paragraphs: The cochlea is the inner-ear structure that converts sound into receptor activity. A cochlear microphonic, or CM, is an electrical response related to the acoustic stimulation of the cochlea, and N1 is the summed activity of primary auditory neurons.

Suga and colleagues recorded both with an electrode at the round window. CM samples receptor-related activity and N1 samples neural discharge, so comparing them locates a response in the receptor stage or the neural stage of peripheral processing.

The recordings used controlled tone bursts with calibrated amplitude at the ear, including 4-ms CM stimuli with rapid rise and decay. Short bursts expose responses at the onset and cessation of a tone and reduce interference from the middle-ear muscle reflex.
inserts.citation: Suga et al. (1975); Wang et al. (2025)
notes: Two electrical signals from the round window sample the receptor and the neural stages of the ear, and their comparison locates where a response arises.
The recording site.
The round window provides a recording site near the cochlea.
The cochlear microphonic follows acoustic stimulation and is a receptor-related signal.
The neural signal.
N1 represents the summed activity of primary auditory neurons.
Recording both allows a receptor-related transient to be compared with a transient in neural discharge.
Controlled stimuli.
Tone bursts were presented with amplitude calibrated at the ear.
Short bursts expose onset and offset effects while reducing interference from the middle-ear muscle reflex.
Interpretation.
Similarity between CM and N1 can support a peripheral origin for a neural response, and the two measurements are not interchangeable.
Round window recording.
Both signals were recorded with an electrode at the round window, so the same site samples receptor-related and neural activity.
Comparing CM and N1 places a response in the receptor stage or the neural stage.
Stimulus design.
Short tone bursts with rapid rise and decay expose onset and cessation responses.
Brief stimuli also reduce interference from the middle-ear muscle reflex.

inserts.title: Single-nucleus sequencing groups cells by RNA
paragraphs: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing measures the RNA associated with individual cell nuclei, so each nucleus has an expression profile. A marker gene helps identify a cell population by its expression pattern, and nuclei with similar profiles are grouped into one population.

Wang and colleagues grouped cochlear nuclei by expression and used more than 200 marker genes to identify neural, sensory, immune and structural populations. They resolved 14 cell types in the horseshoe bat Rhinolophus ferrumequinum and 13 in Myotis pilosus.

Neural populations included two spiral-ganglion categories and glial cells, hair cells and supporting cells occupied the sensory compartment, and marginal and basal cells contributed to the lateral wall. The plotted clusters are molecular groupings, and a firing threshold or preferred frequency would come from recordings of the cells.
notes: A cell atlas assigns identities from gene expression, and the identities name populations whose physiology is measured by other methods.
From RNA to identity.
Single-nucleus sequencing measures RNA associated with individual nuclei.
A marker gene supports the identification of a cell population by its expression pattern.
The populations.
Neural populations included two spiral-ganglion categories and glial cells.
Hair cells and supporting cells occupied the sensory compartment, and marginal and basal cells contributed to lateral-wall categories.
Counts in the two species.
The species-specific analyses resolved 14 cell types in Rhinolophus ferrumequinum and 13 in Myotis pilosus.
More than 200 marker genes supported the identification of the populations.
What the clusters represent.
The plotted expression clusters are molecular groupings, not a map of cochlear position or of frequency tuning.
Marker genes.
A marker gene is expressed in a recognizable pattern, so it helps assign nuclei to a cell population.
More than 200 marker genes were used to identify neural, sensory, immune and structural populations.
Cell types by species.
The analysis resolved 14 cell types in Rhinolophus ferrumequinum and 13 in Myotis pilosus.
Hair cells and supporting cells occupied the sensory compartment, and marginal and basal cells contributed to the lateral wall.

inserts.title: Orthologous genes give a common comparison space
paragraphs: Orthologous genes are corresponding genes in different species inherited from a common ancestral gene. Using orthologs, two species can be placed in the same expression space, so cells of the same kind can be compared directly.

Wang and colleagues used 8607 orthologous genes to build a joint cochlear atlas for the CF bat Rhinolophus ferrumequinum and the FM bat Myotis pilosus. The analysis resolved 26 expression clusters with familiar cochlear identities, including SGNs, glial cells, supporting cells and hair cells.

Some clusters were dominated by one species and others contained both, so the atlas separates shared cellular organization from species-associated expression differences. The two species also differ in ancestry and physiology, and a CF-associated pattern is a candidate adaptation to be tested with wider sampling or direct manipulation.
notes: A shared set of genes gives a controlled way to ask which molecular differences accompany the CF and FM echolocation strategies.
Orthologs.
Orthologous genes descend from a common ancestral gene.
Using them avoids comparing unrelated species-specific marker lists.
The joint atlas.
The joint analysis used 8607 orthologous genes and resolved 26 expression clusters.
The clusters were assigned familiar cochlear identities.
Shared and species-specific signals.
Some clusters were dominated by one species and others included contributions from both.
The separation preserves both shared organization and species differences.
Scope of the comparison.
The two bats differ in ancestry and physiology as well as in echolocation mode, so a CF-associated pattern is a candidate adaptation.
Common comparison space.
Orthologous genes descend from a common ancestral gene, so measuring them in both species places the cells in one expression space.
The joint atlas used 8607 orthologs.
Shared and species-specific clusters.
Some of the 26 clusters were dominated by one species and others contained both.
Shared clusters reflect common cochlear organization, and species-dominated clusters mark expression differences.

inserts.title: Synchrony shapes the population onset response
paragraphs: The envelope is the changing amplitude of a sound or response over time, and it determines how quickly a sound reaches its sustained level. When excitation rises slowly, individual neurons do not fire their first impulses at the same moment.

A summed onset response depends on impulses overlapping in time. If they are spread out, the recorded population peak is smaller even though every neuron remains sensitive, so a weak summed response can reflect dispersed spike timing and not reduced sensitivity.

Suga and colleagues lengthened the rise time of tones away from the resonant band. A 1-ms rise raised the threshold of the summed onset response by approximately 8 dB relative to an abrupt rise, and a 3-ms rise raised it much more, which supports an envelope-based explanation of the apparent threshold shift.
inserts.citation: Suga et al. (1975); Wang et al. (2025)
notes: Population responses depend on both how many neurons respond and how well their impulses line up in time.
Envelope and onset.
The amplitude envelope determines how quickly a sound reaches its sustained level.
Slow rises spread the times of the first impulses across neurons.
Why synchrony matters.
A summed onset potential depends on impulses overlapping in time.
If the impulses are spread out, the recorded peak is smaller without every neuron becoming less responsive.
The test.
Suga and colleagues lengthened the stimulus rise time at frequencies away from resonance.
The onset threshold rose when the sound rose more slowly.
Consequence.
Resonance can alter apparent neural onset sensitivity by changing synchronization.
The frequency at which the largest summed onset response happens to be measured is therefore not the preferred frequency of the whole auditory system.
Rise time and timing.
A slow envelope delays and disperses the first impulses of different neurons.
The summed onset response then has a smaller peak although each neuron stays sensitive.
Size of the effect.
A 1-millisecond rise raised the onset threshold by approximately 8 decibels relative to an abrupt rise, and a 3-millisecond rise raised it much more.

inserts.title: Resonance frequency differs from resting frequency
paragraphs: The resonance frequency is the frequency at which the peripheral resonant system of the ear responds especially strongly. It describes the sensory side of the system, whereas the resting frequency describes the vocal side.

Macías and colleagues measured the resting second-harmonic call frequency in mustached bats, which ranged from 60 to 61.2 kHz, and estimated the resonance frequency, which generally lay above the emitted baseline. They combined acoustic recordings with recordings in the auditory midbrain and examined sharply tuned neurons near the specialized band.

A reference defined from vocal emission therefore need not coincide with a reference defined from the sensory response. The distinction parallels the difference between resting and reference frequencies in the behavioral compensation experiments, and neural tuning was evaluated relative to each individual bat's acoustic and peripheral specialization.
notes: A bat has a sensory frequency reference and a vocal frequency reference, and the two are related but not identical.
Sensory reference.
The resonance frequency is where the peripheral resonant system responds most strongly.
The estimate generally lay above the resting emission.
Vocal reference.
The resting second-harmonic frequency ranged from 60 to 61.2 kHz in these mustached bats.
It is measured from the calls of a stationary animal.
Parallel with compensation.
In compensation experiments the reference frequency of the echo lies slightly above the resting frequency of the call.
The sensory and vocal measures show a similar relationship.
Individual tuning.
Neural tuning was evaluated relative to the acoustic and peripheral specialization of each bat, which avoids assigning one universal CF frequency to the species.
Sensory and vocal references.
The resonance frequency describes the sensory side of the system, and the resting frequency describes the vocal side.
The two need not coincide.
Measurements.
The resting second-harmonic frequency ranged from 60 to 61.2 kilohertz, and the estimated resonance frequency generally lay above it.
Neural recordings in the auditory midbrain examined sharply tuned neurons near the specialized band.

inserts.title: Frequency resolution and time resolution trade off
paragraphs: A spectral–temporal trade-off occurs when finer frequency resolution accompanies poorer temporal resolution. A sharply tuned resonator is an example: it selects a narrow band of frequencies and continues to respond after the sound ends, which extends the peripheral response in time.

Macías and colleagues asked whether this cochlear property constrains duration-selective neurons in the auditory midbrain. They measured frequency bandwidth at 10 dB above threshold and duration bandwidth across stimulus durations in the mustached bat's inferior colliculus.

Resonance-band neurons did not follow the expected relation between narrow frequency tuning and broad duration tuning, whereas neurons outside the specialized band showed the conventional relationship. Central processing can therefore produce sharp temporal filtering despite a peripheral input that is specialized for narrowband frequency analysis.
notes: A trade-off between frequency and time resolution is expected for a tuned system, and the midbrain data test whether it carries through to central neurons.
The trade-off.
Finer frequency resolution accompanies poorer temporal resolution.
Cochlear resonance can sustain activity after sound offset.
The measurements.
Frequency bandwidth was measured at 10 dB above threshold.
Duration bandwidth was measured across stimulus durations.
The result.
Resonance-band neurons did not follow the expected relation between narrow frequency tuning and broad duration tuning.
Neurons outside that specialized band displayed the more conventional relationship.
Interpretation.
The result concerns central response selectivity under controlled pure-tone stimulation, and central processing can sharpen temporal filtering that the periphery does not provide.
Meaning of the trade-off.
A narrowly tuned resonator selects few frequencies and keeps responding after the sound ends.
Fine frequency resolution therefore costs temporal resolution.
The midbrain test.
Frequency bandwidth was measured at 10 decibels above threshold, and duration bandwidth was measured across stimulus durations.
Neurons outside the specialized band followed the conventional relation, and resonance-band neurons did not.

inserts.title: Phase locking represents beat timing
paragraphs: Beats are periodic amplitude fluctuations produced when two tones of slightly different frequency overlap, and their rate depends on the separation between the two frequencies. Phase locking means that a neuron discharges at a consistent phase of a repeating stimulus feature.

Suga and colleagues presented paired tones and recorded whether peripheral impulses followed the resulting fluctuations. Peripheral neurons could phase-lock to beats up to about 3 kHz, so their impulse timing carried information beyond the average number of impulses produced by a tone.

The outgoing signal and its returning echo overlap in time and differ slightly in frequency, so they can produce beats. Phase-locked timing is a potential temporal representation of the frequency difference, alongside the representation supplied by sharply tuned neurons.
notes: Timing and tuning are two ways of representing a frequency difference, and peripheral neurons in the paired-tone experiment carried timing information.
Beats.
Two nearby tone frequencies produce a repeating change in their combined amplitude.
The experiment changed the difference between the tones and measured the times of neural discharge.
Phase locking.
Phase locking is a consistent relation between impulse timing and a phase of the repeating amplitude pattern.
The neurons could follow beat rates up to approximately 3 kilohertz.
Why it matters for echolocation.
Suga and colleagues related the property to overlap between outgoing signals and echoes.
The timing is a potential representation of frequency difference alongside the tuning of individual neurons.
Laboratory signal.
The timing signal is available in the periphery of the laboratory preparation.
Beat rate.
The beat rate depends on the separation between the two tone frequencies, so changing the separation changes how often the amplitude repeats.
Timing beyond spike count.
Impulse timing carried information beyond the average number of impulses produced by a tone.
A temporal code and a tuning code can therefore represent the same frequency difference.

inserts.title: Nonmonotonic responses create level selectivity
paragraphs: A neuron's best amplitude is the sound pressure level that produces its largest response, and it differs from the minimum threshold, which is the weakest effective sound. A nonmonotonic response rises with sound level, reaches a maximum and then falls at stronger levels.

Suga held tone frequency at each cortical neuron's best frequency and counted impulses during 50-ms tones as the level increased. Many CF-region neurons were nonmonotonic, whereas other neurons showed more nearly monotonic growth.

The fall in response at higher levels creates an upper threshold, above which excitation becomes weak or absent. Such neurons are selective for an intermediate level, so frequency and sound level jointly determine which cortical populations are most active.
notes: A neuron that responds most to an intermediate level reports amplitude by its response and not simply by louder meaning more.
Defining the terms.
The best amplitude is the level giving the peak response.
The minimum threshold is the weakest sound that evokes a response and is a different quantity.
The measurement.
Tone frequency was held at the neuron's best frequency while sound level increased.
Some neurons produced more impulses up to an intermediate amplitude and fewer at stronger levels.
The upper threshold.
The loss of excitation at higher levels creates an upper threshold.
Suga related this property to inhibitory interactions elsewhere in the auditory pathway.
Neuron variety.
Other neurons showed more nearly monotonic growth, so the CF region contains neurons with different level functions.
Best amplitude and threshold.
Best amplitude is the level that gives the largest response, and the minimum threshold is the weakest effective level.
The two are different properties of a neuron.
Level selectivity.
A nonmonotonic neuron falls silent or weak above its best level, so it prefers an intermediate level.
Frequency and level together determine which cortical populations are most active.

inserts.title: Pulse interval and duty cycle describe sampling
paragraphs: Pulse interval is the time between consecutive calls, and duty cycle is the proportion of time occupied by sound emission. Both describe how often a bat samples its surroundings and can change independently of the CF frequency.

In Hipposideros armiger, call duration reached about 3–4 ms and pulse interval about 11–12 ms during the final approach to the landing grid. Shortening intervals and shortening calls change duty cycle in different ways, so all three quantities must be measured, and the duty cycle increased during approach.

The sustained CF component was retained while the timing of sampling changed. The bat therefore controlled the returning CF frequency within an acoustic sequence whose temporal structure, harmonic prominence and FM component were also changing.
notes: A bat changes how often it samples and how long each call lasts at the same time that it holds the echo frequency near its reference.
Definitions.
Pulse interval measures the time from one call to the next.
Duty cycle measures how much of the sequence is occupied by emitted sound.
Approach to the landing grid.
Calls became shorter and more closely spaced, with durations of roughly 3 to 4 milliseconds and intervals of roughly 11 to 12 milliseconds.
The sustained CF component was retained.
Why three measures.
Shortening intervals and shortening calls can change duty cycle in different ways.
Duration, interval and duty cycle are therefore measured separately.
Scope.
These measurements describe flight toward a landing target and not prey capture.
Timing of sampling.
Call duration reached about 3 to 4 milliseconds and pulse interval about 11 to 12 milliseconds near the landing grid.
Duty cycle increased during approach.
Independent controls.
Pulse interval and duty cycle can change independently of the CF frequency, so the bat regulates echo frequency while its temporal sampling changes.
